stops.title: Born in Calamba
stops.teaser: A house by the lake, and a mother who teaches
stops.story: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, a farming town on the shore of Laguna de Bay. He was the seventh of eleven children of Francisco Mercado and Teodora Alonso. The family lived in a two-storey bahay na bato near the town church: stone walls below, hardwood and capiz-shell windows above. Part of the ground floor opened to the street for Doña Teodora's small businesses. His mother was his first teacher. She taught him the alphabet when he was about three and read stories to him at night. One story was about a young moth that flew too close to a lamp's flame. Rizal remembered it all his life. From the house he could see Mount Makiling, the mountain that watches over Calamba.

chapters.title: A house by the lake
narration: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda was born in Calamba, Laguna, on Wednesday, 19 June 1861. Years later he noted that it was a few days before the full moon. Calamba was a farming town on the southern shore of Laguna de Bay, the great lake south-east of Manila. Behind it rose Mount Makiling, the mountain that watches over the town.

He was the seventh of eleven children of Francisco Mercado and Teodora Alonso: nine girls and two boys. His only brother, Paciano, was ten years older and would later pay for much of his schooling. Like most families in Calamba, the Mercados farmed land rented from the Dominican estate that owned most of the town, growing rice and sugarcane. Rizal described his family as "neither rich nor poor". By careful saving, his father built a stone house, a bahay na bato, with stone walls below and hardwood and capiz windows above. Capiz is a flat, see-through shell that was used as window glass.

lines.speaker: teodora
lines.text: José, come and look. You can see all of Makiling from here.

fact.text: His second name, Protasio, comes from Saint Protasius, whose feast day is 19 June, the day he was born.

chapters.title: Nights on the azotea
narration: Some of his first memories were of the azotea, the open stone terrace of the house. On moonlit nights he ate supper there. His nurse, who was very fond of him, told stories in which dead people, gold and plants that grew diamonds were all mixed together, and when he would not eat, she threatened to call a bogeyman. At nightfall his mother gathered the children to pray, and then they went out to the azotea or a window to watch the moon.

When he was four, his little sister Concha died. He later wrote that it was the first time he cried out of love and sorrow; until then he had cried only over his own mistakes. He also remembered seeing the Guardia Civil, the colonial police, beat villagers who had failed to take off their hats and bow from a distance. Standing on the lakeshore, he wondered whether people on the far side lived the same way, or whether there, too, one had to bribe the powerful to live in peace.

lines.speaker: jose-child
lines.text: Do the people across the lake live like this too?

fact.text: Rizal wrote about these childhood memories himself, in a memoir he began in 1878, when he was seventeen.

chapters.title: The young moth
narration: His mother, Doña Teodora, was his first teacher. She was well read, understood verse-making, and in later years corrected the poems he brought home at Christmas. One night, with the rest of the family asleep and the room lit by a single coconut-oil lamp, she was teaching him to read from an old Spanish book called The Children's Friend. He read badly, because he did not yet understand Spanish, and his eyes kept drifting to the little moths circling the flame.

So she put the lesson aside and read him a fable instead: an old moth warns a young one not to fly too close to the light. She translated it into Tagalog as she went. As she read, a real moth was singed and fell into the oil. Her warning to her son was clear: do not be disobedient like the young moth. But the boy found that he admired the insect. It had, he wrote, "died a martyr to its illusions". The story never left him. As a grown man he wrote that light is the most beautiful thing in creation, and that it is worth giving one's life for.

chapters.title: First lessons
narration: His education went on at home. His father hired an old man, a former schoolmate of his, to teach José the first steps in Latin; the old teacher lived with the family until he died five months later. The boy drew, modelled small figures in clay, and wrote verses.

In June 1868, just after his sister Trinidad was born, he travelled with his father up the Pasig River to Manila in a casco, a heavy cargo boat. They stopped at Cainta, Taytay and Antipolo, and in Santa Ana he visited his eldest sister, Saturnina, who was studying at La Concordia College. He was happy at every stop along the river. Back in Calamba, his parents decided that their bright, small son needed a real school. His father had been born in Biñan, a larger town to the north, and that is where they would send him.

stops.title: School in Biñan
stops.teaser: First formal school, away from home
stops.story: In June 1869 Paciano took his younger brother José, then eight, to the town of Biñan to go to school. Classes were held in the house of the teacher, Maestro Justiniano Aquino Cruz, a small nipa house near the home of their aunt. Rizal later described him as tall and thin, strict, and very learned in Spanish and Latin grammar. On his first day José was teased, got into a fight with the teacher's son Pedro, and won. He was punished with the ruler more than once, but he soon led the class. An old painter, Juancho Carrera, also taught him to draw and paint. Near the end of 1870 a letter called him home, and he sailed back to Calamba on the steamer Talim. Years later he wrote about the tears he shed on leaving Calamba for Biñan.

chapters.title: Leaving home
narration: One Sunday in 1869, Paciano took his younger brother to Biñan, about an hour and a half away by carriage. Their father had been born there, and he wanted José to go on with the Latin he had begun at home. The parting was tearful for his parents and sisters, but José, as he later wrote, managed to hide his own tears.

They reached Biñan at nightfall and went to the house of an aunt, where José would live. She was over seventy and liked to sit on the floor reading the Bible in Tagalog. Two cousins and three half-cousins lived there too. That first night a cousin walked him around the town under the moon. Biñan seemed large and wealthy to him, but "neither attractive nor cheerful".

lines.text: I will not cry. Not in front of Paciano.

chapters.title: The schoolmaster
narration: The next day Paciano presented him to the teacher, Maestro Justiniano Aquino Cruz, who seemed to have taught Paciano too. Rizal remembered him as tall and thin, with a long neck and a sharp nose, his body leaning slightly forward, in a shirt of sinamay, a light cloth woven by women in Batangas. He knew Latin and Spanish grammar by heart, and he was very strict. Classes were held in his own house, about thirty metres from the aunt's home.

The teacher's first questions were short, and Rizal wrote them down years later. Because the new boy answered "a little" to both, the teacher's son, older and taller than José, began to make fun of him. The two boys fought. Somehow, José bent the bigger boy down over the class benches, then let him go, having hurt only his pride. Soon after, another boy challenged him to wrestle. This time José lost, and nearly cracked his head on the pavement.

chapters.title: A day in Biñan
narration: Rizal kept a careful record of his days. He heard Mass at four in the morning if there was one, or studied first and went to Mass afterwards. Then he looked for mabolo fruit in the yard. Breakfast was usually a plate of rice and two dried sardines. Class ran until ten; after lunch came a study period, then school again from two until five. Supper was rice with ayungin, a small fish from the lake, followed by prayers and, on moonlit nights, games in the street with his cousins.

He was punished often. Rare were the days, he wrote, without five or six blows of the ruler on his hand, yet he usually won the class competitions. Near the school lived the teacher's father-in-law, an old painter called Juancho, who let José help with his paintings. José and another pupil, José Guevarra, became known as the "class painters".

lines.speaker: jose-boy
lines.text: Rice and two dried sardines, then class until ten.

lines.speaker: jose-boy

chapters.title: The steamer Talim
narration: Late in 1870 a letter came from his sister Saturnina: the steamer Talim would stop at Biñan to bring him home. He said goodbye to his friends and thanked his teacher. Looking back, he decided that the maestro had punished him out of kindness, and that "his heart was heavy when he did it".

He left on Saturday afternoon, 17 December 1870. It was the first steamer he had ever seen, and he thought it beautiful. He was the only passenger from Biñan. A Frenchman, Arturo Camps, a friend of his father, looked after him on board. When Calamba's shore came into view he wanted to jump into the first banca; a deckhand lifted him into the captain's boat, four sailors rowed them ashore, and a servant was waiting with a carriage. He found himself home again, "happy in the love of my family". His time in Biñan had lasted only about a year and a half, but he had learned Latin and Spanish grammar, and that he could hold his own among older boys.

stops.title: First day at the Ateneo
stops.teaser: A small boy, a big school, two rival "empires"
stops.story: In June 1872, eleven-year-old José went to Manila to enter the Ateneo Municipal, a school run by Jesuit priests inside the walls of Intramuros. At first the school turned him away. He had registered late, and he looked small and sickly. With help from Manuel Xerez Burgos, he was accepted. The Jesuits split each class into two rival ‘empires’, Romans and Carthaginians, who competed for the top places. José began at the bottom and rose to ‘emperor’ within a month. He studied Spanish, Latin, mathematics and the sciences, and he began writing poems. In March 1877 he finished with a Bachelor of Arts and the highest grades, called sobresaliente. Years later he said his time at the Ateneo shaped how he thought and worked.

chapters.title: A family in trouble
narration: The years after Biñan were hard. In 1871, Teodora's brother José Alberto took back his wife after she had left him and their children. Within days she accused him of trying to poison her, and named Teodora as his accomplice. Rizal believed the charge was false and the officials unfair. His mother was arrested and jailed, and the case dragged on for about two and a half years before two of Manila's leading lawyers proved her innocent.

Then, on 17 February 1872, three Filipino priests, Mariano Gómez, José Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, were executed at Bagumbayan, accused of leading a mutiny at the Cavite arsenal. Many Filipinos believed they were innocent. Paciano had been close to Father Burgos. Fearing that the family name would attract attention, the family had José enrolled under the name Rizal instead of Mercado.

chapters.title: Turned away at the door
narration: On 10 June 1872 José went to Manila and took his entrance examinations at the College of San Juan de Letran, in Christian doctrine, arithmetic and reading. He passed. But when he went to the Ateneo Municipal, the Jesuit school inside the walls of Intramuros, the priest in charge refused him. He had come late, he did not look strong, and he was very small for eleven. Then Manuel Xerez Burgos, a nephew of the executed Father Burgos, spoke in his favour, and the school let him in.

He put on the uniform, a white coat and a necktie, heard Mass in the Jesuits' chapel and walked into his first class. His teacher was Father José Bech: tall, thin and quick in his movements, sometimes cross and impatient, at other times, Rizal wrote, "playing like a child".

fact.text: The Ateneo Municipal stood on Calle Arzobispo, inside the walled city of Intramuros.

chapters.title: The rival empires
narration: The Jesuits split each class into two rival "empires" that competed in every lesson. The best student on each side was its "emperor". Rizal's memoir calls the two sides Romans and Greeks; many later books say Romans and Carthaginians. José was put at the end of the line. He understood Spanish but could barely speak it. So he paid three pesos a month for extra lessons at Santa Isabel College during the siesta hour. By the end of the first week he was moving up. A month later, he was emperor, and he won his first prize, a religious picture.

He lodged at first outside the walls, on Calle Caraballo, a twenty-five-minute walk away, in the house of a woman who owed his family three hundred pesos. Later he moved inside Intramuros. In his second year he found three old classmates from Biñan in his class, and at the end of the year he won a medal. A year later, slips in his spoken Spanish cost him the medal, which went to a Spanish boy who spoke his mother tongue better. He read eagerly: at twelve he was thrilled by The Count of Monte Cristo, and he persuaded his father to buy him a set of world histories, saying he needed them for school.

chapters.title: Sobresaliente
narration: During vacations he visited his mother in prison. Once, after not seeing her for more than a year, he surprised her, and they wept in each other's arms. Another time he told her of a dream that, he said, meant she would be free within three months. He wrote that the prediction came true. When she was released, she came straight to embrace him.

At the Ateneo a new teacher, Father Francisco de Paula Sánchez, encouraged him to study hard and to write. Rizal carved a small image of the Sacred Heart from wood, and wrote poems, among them one in praise of education as the light of a country. On 14 March 1877 he received his Bachelor of Arts with the highest rating, sobresaliente (excellent). He was fifteen.

stops.title: University in Intramuros
stops.story: In 1877 Rizal entered the University of Santo Tomas, run by Dominican friars inside the walls of Intramuros. He first took philosophy and letters, then in 1878 he moved to medicine, partly because his mother's eyes were failing. He did not enjoy the school. He later wrote that the Dominican teachers were hostile to Filipino students and that the teaching was old-fashioned. Outside class he did well. In 1879 the Liceo Artístico-Literario of Manila held a poetry contest for native and mestizo writers. Rizal, eighteen, won first prize with "A la juventud filipina", a poem calling the Filipino youth the "fair hope" of the motherland. His prize was a silver pen shaped like a feather. In May 1882 he quietly left to finish his studies in Spain.

chapters.title: What to study?
narration: After the Ateneo, Rizal had to choose a career. His father wanted him to go on studying. His mother did not want him to go back to Manila at all, saying he already had enough education. Rizal later wondered whether she had a presentiment of what learning would cost him. In 1877 he enrolled at the University of Santo Tomas, run by Dominican friars inside Intramuros, in philosophy and letters. He was only sixteen. He admitted he was so little interested in metaphysics that he did not even buy the textbook.

At the same time he took a course in land surveying at the Ateneo and passed the examination. He was too young to receive the title of surveyor, which was granted to him only in 1881. Even while at Santo Tomas, he kept returning to the Ateneo, where he felt more at home.

chapters.title: Medicine, for his mother
narration: On one visit home for the holidays, he walked into the house and his mother did not recognise him. She was losing her sight. In 1878 he changed his course to medicine, hoping one day to treat her eyes.

He did not enjoy the university. He felt that the Dominican professors were hostile to Filipino students, and that their teaching was old-fashioned compared with the Jesuits'. His marks in medicine were mostly "good" and "fair", with "excellent" in chemistry and therapeutics: respectable, but not the brilliance he showed in languages and letters. Rivalry between the two religious orders, and his reputation as a Jesuit-trained prize-winner, did not help. Quarrels between Filipino and Spanish students were common, and Rizal led a students' group, the Compañerismo, formed to stand up for Filipino students.

chapters.title: The silver pen
narration: Outside class he shone. In 1879 the Liceo Artístico-Literario of Manila, a society of art and letters, held a poetry contest for native and mestizo writers. Rizal, eighteen, won first prize with "A la juventud filipina" (To the Filipino Youth). The poem urged young Filipinos to use their talents and called them the "fair hope" of the motherland. It was a bold idea for its time: a native-born writer speaking of the Philippines as the patria, the homeland, of Filipinos. His prize was a silver pen shaped like a feather.

The next year he entered another Liceo contest, held to honour the Spanish writer Cervantes, with an allegory called "El consejo de los dioses" (The Council of the Gods). Biographers agree that it was judged an outstanding entry. They disagree about what happened next. Russell and Rodriguez wrote that the prize was taken from him once the judges learned he was a Filipino; others say he received it, but that Spaniards in Manila resented losing to a native.

chapters.title: A wound and a decision
narration: On 8 December 1880 a student society at the Ateneo staged his play "Junto al Pasig" (Beside the Pasig), on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, a big day in the school's calendar. In it he put criticism of Spain into the mouth of the devil, a joke the authorities did not miss. Around the same time, on vacation in Calamba, he passed a dark figure in the street one night without saluting. It was a lieutenant of the Guardia Civil, who struck him across the back with his sword. Rizal complained to the authorities, and nothing came of it.

By 1882 he and Paciano had made a secret plan: he would finish his studies in Spain, where he could learn freely and observe how Europe lived. His brother would find the money; a sister gave him a diamond ring to pawn if he needed it. He would not tell his parents; Paciano would explain once he was safely away. On 3 May 1882, before dawn, he sailed.

chapters.title: A secret departure
narration: Rizal left Manila on 3 May 1882 aboard the steamer Salvadora, travelling under the name José Mercado. His parents were not told. Only his brother, a few relatives and some friends knew. To avoid suspicion he first went home to Calamba as if on an ordinary visit, then slipped back to Manila and boarded after midnight. By daybreak he was on his way to Singapore. After he was gone, Paciano had to pretend to search Manila for his missing brother.

Why such secrecy? A student who left the colony to study abroad without the authorities' approval could bring suspicion on his whole family, and the Mercados were already watched. Once his absence was discovered, relatives in Calamba were followed and questioned. Money for the journey came from Paciano and an uncle, and was later sent to him through a cousin in Manila, so that the estate's managers would not learn of it.

chapters.title: Across the seas
narration: With a sketchbook in hand, he drew his fellow passengers and kept a diary of everything he saw. At Singapore he changed to the French mail steamer Djemnah. He crossed the Indian Ocean, stopped at Aden, and sailed through the Suez Canal, which had opened only thirteen years before. From Marseille he took the train across the Pyrenees mountains into Spain. At the frontier town of Port Bou, he noted, the Spanish customs officers reminded him of the worst kind of official in Manila. On 16 June 1882 he reached Barcelona.

In Marseille, before the train, he found time to visit the Château d'If, the island prison made famous by The Count of Monte Cristo, the novel that had thrilled him as a schoolboy. He also noticed how differently he was treated on each side of the border: courteously by French officials, coldly by Spanish ones.

chapters.title: A city that spoke freely
narration: Filipino students in Barcelona, some of them his old Ateneo classmates, welcomed him at a café on the Plaza de Cataluña. They met only every other Sunday, because few could afford cafés more often. They asked for news from Manila, and he had to tell them that little had changed: the old abuses went on and the same kind of officials were in charge.

He stayed at the Fonda de España and walked the Rambla, the city's long, tree-lined avenue. At first he did not like Barcelona; within weeks he changed his mind. What struck him most was the freedom. Catalans criticised the government openly, newspapers printed things that in Manila would have meant prison, and republican clubs hung signs on their doors. The same flag flew over Barcelona and Manila, but the rights under it were not the same. In Barcelona, he noticed, people were ready to stand up for their rights.

chapters.title: Love of Country
narration: In Barcelona he wrote "Amor Patrio" (Love of Country), his first essay written abroad. In it he asked Filipinos to love their country above everything, and to work for it. He signed it with a pen name, Laong Laan, meaning "ever prepared". It was published in Manila on 20 August 1882 in Diariong Tagalog, a new newspaper printed in both Spanish and Tagalog; the Tagalog version was translated by Marcelo H. del Pilar.

Soon a letter came from Paciano. Cholera had broken out in Manila, and he advised José to stay in Spain and finish medicine in Madrid, the capital. In the autumn of 1882 Rizal left Barcelona for the Universidad Central. Craig suggests that his short stay in Barcelona also let him put his travel papers in order before he entered a national university.

"Amor Patrio" was followed by a second article for the same paper, "Los Viajes" (Travels), on what a young person can learn by seeing other countries. He was already thinking like a reporter for his people: everything he saw abroad, he measured against home.

chapters.title: The Universidad Central
narration: In the autumn of 1882 Rizal reached Madrid and enrolled at the Universidad Central, the leading university of Spain, on Calle de San Bernardo. He took two full courses at once: medicine, and philosophy and letters. As if that were not enough, he studied painting and sculpture at an academy of fine arts, took private lessons in languages, and practised fencing and shooting.

He believed in living by a timetable. He divided his day into blocks, with one set aside for general reading: French classics, Shakespeare, Goethe, books on politics, and above all history. Languages came easily to someone raised speaking Tagalog and Spanish who had learned Latin and Greek at school. In Madrid he added French, English and Italian, and began German.

chapters.title: Living on little
narration: He had left Manila with about seven hundred pesos and a diamond ring. After that, money came from his father and Paciano each month, sent through a cousin in Manila so that the estate's managers in Calamba would not learn of it. It was never much, and in 1884 and 1885, when times were hard at home, it often came late. He lived simply, ate little, and spent most of what he had on books, many of them second-hand. Among them was a Spanish volume on the lives of the presidents of the United States, which he read until it was nearly worn out: men born poor who rose to lead their country.

He allowed himself a few pleasures: the theatre, when his purse allowed, and a lottery ticket now and then, bought in small amounts but regularly. Most Filipino students in Madrid knew him as courteous and brilliant but rarely seen in cafés. When he did join them, they said, he was the life of the table.

chapters.title: The idea of a novel
narration: In Madrid he read two novels that changed his plans: Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin, about slavery in the United States, and Eugène Sue's The Wandering Jew, about the suffering of the poor. He saw how a story could move a whole nation. In January 1884, at a gathering of Filipinos in Madrid, he proposed that they write a book together about the Philippines, each taking a subject. The others liked the idea, but almost everyone wanted to write about Filipino women, and no one wanted the hard subjects.

Disappointed, he decided to write the book alone. Near the end of 1884 he began a novel about life in the Philippines under Spanish rule. By the time he left Madrid, about half of what would become Noli Me Tangere was written.

chapters.title: A toast to genius
narration: On 25 June 1884 the Filipino community in Madrid held a banquet to honour two Filipino painters who had just won top prizes at the National Exposition of Fine Arts: Juan Luna, a gold medal for his painting Spoliarium, and Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, a silver medal. Rizal gave the main speech. Its message was that talent is not the property of one race: Luna and Hidalgo proved that Filipinos could stand beside the best artists in Europe.

That same week, on 21 June 1884, he earned his licentiate in medicine, the degree that allowed him to practise. A year later, on 19 June 1885, his twenty-fourth birthday, he completed his licentiate in philosophy and letters with the rating "excellent". He also finished the courses for a doctorate in medicine, but could not afford the fees, so the doctor's diploma was never issued. In Madrid he also became a Freemason, joining a lodge called Acacia. With two degrees in hand, he set out to study the eye.

Madrid also gave him friends among liberal Spaniards who wanted reform at home. Craig records that in later years he played chess with Francisco Pi y Margall, a former president of Spain's short-lived republic and a champion of education for all.

He wrote home that he could now perform all the operations, though they needed a lot of practice. In his free time he visited Filipino friends, among them the painter Juan Luna and the Pardo de Tavera family. Paris was expensive, and he lived carefully. On 1 February 1886 he left for Germany to continue his training.

chapters.title: An eye doctor for his mother
narration: With his two degrees, Rizal chose to specialise in ophthalmology, the medicine of the eye. The reason was personal: his mother was going blind, and he wanted to be able to treat her. After a tour of the Spanish countryside, where he studied village life and thought the peasants looked like characters from Don Quixote, he reached Paris in the autumn of 1885.
Paris was the most modern city he had yet seen, and one of the most expensive. He lived carefully, counting every franc, and spent his money on books, lessons and his training.

He had a plan for his years abroad, which Russell and Rodriguez describe: to visit the leading countries of Europe, study their institutions, learn the secrets of their progress, and carry those lessons home to his people. Medicine would give him a living and a way to serve; the rest of his time would go to that larger study.

chapters.title: In Dr. de Wecker's clinic
narration: From November 1885 to February 1886 he worked as an assistant to Dr. Louis de Wecker, one of the leading eye surgeons in France and the author of a standard textbook on the eye. Patients came to his clinic from across Europe. Rizal watched de Wecker diagnose and operate, examined patients with the ophthalmoscope, a lamp-and-mirror tool for looking inside the eye, and learned to operate himself. Craig writes that he became de Wecker's favourite pupil.

He wrote home that he could now perform all the operations, though each one needed a great deal of practice. He paid particular attention to the eye diseases that were most common in the Philippines and least understood there.

His mother's illness was a cataract, a clouding of the lens inside the eye that slowly blurs sight until a person can see only light and shadow. The cure was surgery to remove the clouded lens, a delicate operation that a surgeon must practise many times before trying it on a patient, let alone on his own mother.

chapters.title: Friends in Paris
narration: In his free hours he visited the Filipinos of Paris. The Pardo de Tavera family had lived there since 1872, when they were exiled after the Cavite mutiny. The brothers Trinidad and Félix became close friends, and their mother shared her memories of official life in Manila. Rizal also spent much time in the studio of the painter Juan Luna, who married Paz Pardo de Tavera in 1886.

Luna used his friend as a model. Rizal posed as an Egyptian priest in Luna's painting The Death of Cleopatra, and as the chieftain Sikatuna in The Blood Compact, a painting of the sixteenth-century friendship pact between Sikatuna and the Spaniard Legazpi. The two friends argued about art and politics and fenced on Sundays.

Trinidad Pardo de Tavera loved the study of languages and Félix loved art; both shared Rizal's belief that education was the way forward for their people. The painting of the Blood Compact also carried a message. The pact of 1565, sealed with drops of blood in wine, recalled a time when a Spaniard and a Filipino had met as equals, a promise reformers felt Spain had long since broken.

chapters.title: Toward Germany
narration: At night he wrote. About a quarter of his novel was written in Paris. He also kept up his German lessons, because Germany had some of the best medical schools in Europe, and life there was cheaper than in Paris.
On 1 February 1886 he left Paris by train. Two days later, on 3 February, he arrived in Heidelberg, an old university town in south-western Germany, to continue his training in the eye.

Between the clinic and his desk, he also visited the city's great museums and galleries, studying art as carefully as medicine. Paris, he found, rewarded curiosity, but it emptied a student's purse quickly.

chapters.title: The old university town

His housemates proposed him for the town's chess club, where he was registered, by mistake, as a law student like them. The club's matches drew large crowds, and he was a strong player; Craig says he left a record among the experts.

chapters.title: Professor Becker's clinic
narration: His work was at the University Eye Hospital under Professor Otto Becker, a leading German eye specialist. He examined patients, watched operations and assisted where he could, and attended lectures in medicine and other subjects.

He also watched German life closely and wrote home about it. In a letter to his sister Trinidad he admired German women as serious, hard-working and well educated, and hoped Filipino women would have the same chance to study. He liked the German custom of introducing oneself at gatherings instead of waiting to be introduced, and the order and cleanliness of German towns.

German universities then led the world in medical research, and Heidelberg's eye clinic was among the best. For Rizal, it was a chance to learn the newest methods of examining and operating on the eye, the very skills he hoped to use on his mother.

chapters.title: To the flowers of Heidelberg
narration: In spring the banks of the Neckar filled with flowers, among them his favourite, the small light-blue forget-me-not. Homesick, he wrote a poem, "A las flores de Heidelberg" (To the Flowers of Heidelberg). In it he asks the foreign flowers to travel to his homeland and carry his love to everyone he left behind: peace to his country, faith for its sons and virtue for its daughters.

He describes himself walking by the cold Neckar at dawn, greeting the sun as it rises over the Königstuhl hill, and remembering that at that very hour it is shining at noon over the Philippines. He pressed some of the flowers between the pages of a book, as the poem says, to keep them.

He sent the poem home in a letter. The forget-me-not was a fitting choice: in Europe the little flower stood for remembrance and faithful love, exactly what a homesick traveller wanted to say to the people he had left behind.

chapters.title: A letter to Leitmeritz
narration: On 31 July 1886, from Heidelberg, Rizal wrote in German to Ferdinand Blumentritt, a schoolteacher in Leitmeritz, Bohemia, who had studied the peoples and languages of the Philippines for years without ever going there. With the letter he sent a gift: a small arithmetic book printed in both Spanish and Tagalog.

Blumentritt replied warmly, sending books in return. It was the start of a friendship carried on almost entirely by letter. The two men wrote to each other for ten years, about science, books, politics and their families, until the night before Rizal died. In early August the university celebrated its five-hundredth anniversary, and soon afterwards Rizal left Heidelberg for Leipzig, arriving on 14 August.

Blumentritt, born in Prague in 1853, taught at the secondary school in Leitmeritz. He read Spanish and had written widely on the peoples and languages of the Philippines, though he never set foot there. He would become Rizal's most trusted adviser, and later wrote the introduction to Rizal's edition of Morga's history of the Philippines.

Rizal was a Catholic, but he and the pastor became close friends. They talked often about religion and found they agreed on many things. The quiet village helped him work. Here he wrote the last chapters of his first novel, Noli Me Tangere. His German also improved. On 25 June 1886 he returned to Heidelberg. Today the village remembers him with a park named after him.

chapters.title: Into the hills
narration: In the spring of 1886 Rizal left the town for a while and went up into the Odenwald, the wooded hills above Heidelberg, to the village of Wilhelmsfeld, about ten kilometres away. It was quiet, green and cheap, and the clean air was good for working. Farms, forest paths and a small church were nearly all there was. For a writer with a novel to finish, it was ideal.
He found lodgings in the vicarage, the pastor's house, and stayed for about three months.
Rizal had arrived in Germany only that February. His German was still halting, and living with a German family meant speaking it from breakfast to bedtime.

chapters.title: The pastor's house
narration: The pastor was Karl Ullmer, a Protestant minister, who lived with his wife and their two children, Etta and Fritz. Rizal was a Catholic, and in the Philippines Catholics were taught to fear Protestants. Yet he and the pastor became close friends. In the evenings they talked about religion and found that they agreed on much more than they disagreed. Both believed that faith should lead to kindness and tolerance, not to hatred between churches.
The family treated him as one of their own, and living in a German household made his German better every week.

The friendship meant more because of the times. In the Philippines, the friars warned their flocks that Protestants were heretics to be avoided. Germany itself had long been divided between Catholic and Protestant regions. For a Filipino Catholic and a German Lutheran pastor to share a table, and their beliefs, openly and with respect, was unusual.

chapters.title: The last chapters
narration: The quiet hills let him work. In Wilhelmsfeld he wrote the last chapters of his first novel, Noli Me Tangere. The novel had been growing for two years, in Madrid, in Paris and in Heidelberg. Now it was nearly complete.

The friendship with Pastor Ullmer may have shaped how he wrote about religion. In his novel, Rizal attacks abusive friars and the misuse of the Church's power over people's lives, but not faith itself. Those who knew him in Germany saw a man who was critical of the religious orders in his country yet deeply respectful of sincere belief, wherever he found it.

The book's title, Noli Me Tangere, is Latin for "Touch me not", words from the Gospel of John. Its hero, Crisóstomo Ibarra, returns to the Philippines after seven years of study in Europe, hoping to build a school in his town, and runs into the power of a friar and the colonial officials who protect him. Through Ibarra's story, Rizal set out to show the "social cancer" of his country so that it could be cured.

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: It is not faith I write against, but the men who use it to rule.

chapters.title: Remembered in the village
narration: On 25 June 1886 Rizal said goodbye to the Ullmers and returned to Heidelberg. A few weeks later he wrote his first letter to Ferdinand Blumentritt, and in August he left for Leipzig.

Wilhelmsfeld has not forgotten its guest. The village keeps a park named after him, with a monument, and Filipinos living in Germany come to visit it. For a stay of only three months, it left a long trace: a finished novel, a lasting friendship, and a lesson in tolerance that Rizal carried for the rest of his life.

His German was now good enough for scholarly work. A year later in Berlin he would read a paper in German on Tagalog poetry before a learned society, something hard to imagine without those months of daily German in a pastor's home.
Rizal spent much of his life on the move, and many of the places he passed through kept no trace of him. Wilhelmsfeld is one of the few small places that did.

One was Friedrich Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell, the story of a Swiss hero who stood up to unjust rulers, so that Filipinos could read about a fight for freedom. Another was a set of fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen, for his nieces and nephews. Historians do not fully agree on where each translation was started and finished. On 29 October 1886 he left Leipzig for Dresden, and then went on to Berlin.

chapters.title: City of books
narration: Rizal arrived in Leipzig, in the Kingdom of Saxony, on 14 August 1886. Leipzig was the capital of the German book trade, full of publishers, printers and bookshops, and home to a famous university. He attended lectures there, especially in history and psychology, a young science that Leipzig was then making famous.

He made friends among the scholars, among them the historian and geographer Friedrich Ratzel and the anthropologist Hans Meyer. They talked about how history, language and surroundings shape a people, questions that mattered to anyone trying to understand his own country.

It was a short stay of less than three months, but a busy one. Leipzig's university had opened the world's first laboratory of experimental psychology in 1879, and students came from many countries to study the new science of the mind. Craig suggests that what Rizal learned there helped him think about how a people's character is shaped by its history and treatment, not fixed by race.

chapters.title: Tell, in Tagalog
narration: In Germany he took on two translations into Tagalog. The first was Wilhelm Tell, a play by the German poet Friedrich Schiller about a Swiss hero who stood up to a cruel foreign governor and helped his people win their freedom. Rizal wanted Filipinos to read, in their own language, a story about a people resisting tyranny.

Historians do not fully agree on where the translation was begun and finished. Some textbooks place it in Leipzig; others link it to Heidelberg and Wilhelmsfeld. The scholar Ramon Guillermo, who studied the translation closely, dates it to 1886.

In the play, the Austrian governor Gessler forces Tell to shoot an apple from his own son's head. Tell succeeds, later frees his people from Gessler, and becomes a symbol of the Swiss struggle for liberty. Rizal also cared about Tagalog itself: he thought it should be written in a spelling suited to its own sounds, not forced into Spanish rules, and translating a classic was a way to show that Tagalog could carry great literature.

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: A people who read about freedom in their own language will not forget it.

fact.text: Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell was first staged in 1804.

chapters.title: Stories for the children
narration: The second translation was for his nieces and nephews at home: a set of fairy tales by the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen. He wrote them out neatly by hand and illustrated them with his own drawings, as if making a real book, with a dedication to the children's father.

Rizal believed that children should grow up reading good stories in their own language. In letters he urged the children to study, and corrected their grammar gently. His translations were a way of teaching from far away.

His advice to the young was always the same. Years later, from Dapitan, he wrote to a nephew: "Learn, learn and think much about what you learn." Life, he added, goes well only for those who have both intelligence and heart.

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: For my nieces and nephews: a book in Tagalog, with pictures.

fact.text: The Andersen translations filled some forty handwritten, illustrated pages.

chapters.title: Living cheaply
narration: Of all the German cities he lived in, Leipzig was the cheapest, and he needed every saving. He earned some money correcting proofs for a publishing house, which also taught him how books were made and printed. He kept fit with exercise, and kept writing.

On 29 October 1886 he left Leipzig for Dresden, where he met Dr. Adolf Bernhard Meyer, director of the museum of anthropology and ethnography, who had studied the Philippines himself. In Dresden's art museum he saw a painting of Prometheus Bound, the Greek hero chained for bringing fire to people, which moved him deeply. From Dresden he went on to Berlin, the capital of the German Empire, arriving at the start of November.

Berlin was the heart of German science, the home of famous anthropologists and medical researchers. Rizal hoped to learn from them, and to finish, at last, the novel he had carried across three countries.

stops.title: The Noli is printed

Then his friend Dr. Maximo Viola, a fellow Filipino from Bulacan, came to visit. Viola lent him the money to print it. In March 1887, the first 2,000 copies came off the press in Berlin. Rizal sent copies to friends, including Ferdinand Blumentritt. The novel spread quietly to the Philippines, where the Spanish authorities banned it. It made Rizal famous, and a target.

chapters.title: The capital of science
narration: Rizal arrived in Berlin, capital of the new German Empire, at the start of November 1886. He came for three reasons: to learn more medicine, to meet the scholars who studied his part of the world, and to finish his novel. He worked in the eye clinic of Dr. Karl Ernst Schweigger and attended lectures at the University of Berlin.

In Berlin he met Fedor Jagor, a traveller whose book on the Philippines he had read as a student in Manila. Jagor had predicted that Spain would one day lose the islands, and that the United States might take its place. Jagor introduced him to Rudolf Virchow, a famous doctor, anthropologist and democrat, who welcomed Rizal into the Berlin Anthropological Society. In April 1887 Rizal read a paper in German on the art of Tagalog verse before the Ethnographic Society of Berlin. A Filipino was teaching German scholars about Filipino poetry, in their own language.

Jagor's book had appeared in German in 1873. Virchow, besides being a great scientist, sat in the German parliament, where he opposed the powerful chancellor Bismarck. Rizal admired how such a man could serve both science and his people.

lines.text: They study my country from books. I can show them it from the inside.

chapters.title: A winter of hunger
narration: He rented a cheap room on the third floor of a lodging house near the university and worked late into the night, rewriting and finishing the last part of the novel. Money from home was late again. That winter he grew so poor that he ate once a day, sometimes only bread, and wore his clothes until they were thin. He washed his own clothes and cleaned his own room.

The printer's price was low by European standards, but he could not pay even that. Biographers say that in a moment of despair he nearly threw the manuscript into the fire. Five years of work, written in Madrid, Paris, Heidelberg, Wilhelmsfeld and Berlin, almost ended in a Berlin stove.

chapters.title: A friend's loan
narration: Then a friend arrived: Dr. Máximo Viola, a young Filipino doctor from San Miguel, Bulacan, who was touring Europe. He found Rizal in poverty, with a finished manuscript and no money. Viola offered to lend him the money to print it, and Rizal accepted. To bring the cost down, Rizal cut parts of the book, including a whole chapter.

The printer was the Berliner Buchdruckerei-Actien-Gesellschaft, a printing company that charged far less than printers in Spain. Viola helped read the proofs. In March 1887 the first 2,000 copies came off the press. Rizal gave Viola the corrected proofs, the pen he had used, and one of the first copies, with a dedication thanking him as the first to read and appreciate the work. When money came from Paciano, Rizal paid him back.

chapters.title: Touch me not
narration: The title, Noli Me Tangere, is Latin for "Touch me not", words from the Gospel of John. Rizal dedicated the book "To My Country". In the dedication he compares his country's troubles to a cancer so painful that people avoid touching it, and says he will lift the veil to show the disease, so that a cure can be found.

He sent the first copies to friends: to Blumentritt in Leitmeritz, and to Filipino reformers in Spain. Copies were smuggled into the Philippines, where the authorities soon banned the book and the friars condemned it. Yet people read it in secret, sometimes passing one copy around a whole town. The novel made Rizal famous among Filipinos and marked him as a dangerous man in the eyes of the colonial government.
Rizal wrote the novel in Spanish on purpose. Educated Filipinos read Spanish, and so did the officials and lawmakers in Spain whom he hoped would see, at last, what was happening in their colony.

lines.speaker: rizal

fact.text: The 1912 English translation by Charles Derbyshire was titled The Social Cancer.

stops.title: Meeting Blumentritt
stops.story: Rizal and Ferdinand Blumentritt had written to each other for almost a year, but they had never met. In May 1887, after the Noli was printed, Rizal and his friend Maximo Viola set out on a tour of Europe. On 13 May 1887 their train reached Leitmeritz in Bohemia, then part of Austria-Hungary, and Blumentritt was waiting at the station. He helped them find a room at the Hotel Krebs and took them home to meet his wife Rosa and their children. For four days he showed them his town, its beer gardens and its old square. On 16 May 1887 Rizal and Viola signed the city's memorial book after meeting the mayor. The two friends met only this once, but they wrote to each other until the night before Rizal died.

chapters.title: A grand tour
narration: With the Noli printed, Rizal and Máximo Viola set out in May 1887 on a tour of central Europe. They left Berlin by train, passed through Dresden, and on 13 May 1887 reached Leitmeritz, a small town on the Elbe River in Bohemia, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. It is now Litoměřice, in the Czech Republic.

Rizal and Ferdinand Blumentritt had written to each other for nearly a year, but had never met. Blumentritt was waiting at the station. Biographers say he recognised his friend from a pencil sketch of himself that Rizal had sent him. The first meeting of two friends who knew each other only from letters was warm from the first moment.
Viola later wrote down his memories of travelling with Rizal, and his account is one of the main sources for these weeks.

lines.text: Professor, after a year of letters, I feel I have known you all my life.

chapters.title: The Blumentritt home
narration: Blumentritt helped them find rooms at the Hotel Krebs and brought them home to meet his family: his wife, Rosa, and their children. Rosa cooked for the visitors, and they spent long evenings at the professor's table. Rizal drew a quick sketch of his host on a scrap of paper, so lifelike that Blumentritt kept it for the rest of his life.

The two men talked about the Philippines for hours. Blumentritt knew the names of its peoples, languages and islands from years of study; Rizal knew the life behind them. For four days Blumentritt showed them his town: its old square, its churches and its beer gardens.

Blumentritt's knowledge came from Spanish books, old maps and a network of correspondents. Rizal brought what no book could give him: the view of a Filipino who had grown up in the places Blumentritt had only read about.

lines.speaker: blumentritt
lines.text: Tell me about Calamba. I know it only as a dot on my maps.

lines.speaker: viola
lines.text: Careful, Professor. Once José starts on Calamba, he does not stop.

fact.text: Craig writes that the sketch was preserved among the Rizal relics Blumentritt treasured.

chapters.title: A speech in German
narration: Blumentritt took Rizal to a meeting of the town's tourist club, a society that promoted the beauty of the region. Rizal was invited to speak, and he addressed the members in fluent German. They were impressed that a visitor from the far side of the world could speak their language so well, and on their own subject. Craig notes that Rizal was always interested in how other countries attracted travellers, an idea he hoped the Philippines would one day use.

The visitors also met the mayor. On 16 May 1887 Rizal and Viola signed the town's memorial book, which can still be seen today with their signatures. In just a few days, a stranger had been made welcome by a whole town.

Leitmeritz was a German-speaking town in a mostly Czech land. The Austro-Hungarian Empire was home to many peoples, Germans, Czechs, Hungarians, Poles and others, who often argued about language and rights. Rizal, who came from a colony, followed such questions with great interest.

chapters.title: Friends for life
narration: After four days the travellers left for Prague, carrying letters of introduction from Blumentritt. They went on to Vienna, where they met the novelist Norfenfals, then travelled up the Danube, through Munich and Nuremberg, and into Switzerland. In Geneva, in June, Viola turned back toward Barcelona, and Rizal went on to Italy, and Rome.

Rizal and Blumentritt never met again. But they wrote to each other until the night before Rizal died, and Blumentritt became his most trusted friend: he wrote the introduction to Rizal's edition of Morga's history, defended him in print, and grieved for him all his life. From Marseille, on 3 July 1887, Rizal sailed for home.

In Rome he toured the ruins of the ancient city, and on 29 June, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, he visited the Vatican. Then he made his way to Marseille. He had been away from home for five years, and he had a novel to show for it.

The Governor-General called him to Malacañang and gave him a Spanish officer as a bodyguard. Rizal also helped the farmers of Calamba prepare a report on their troubles with the Dominican estate that owned their land. To protect his family, he left again on 3 February 1888.

chapters.title: Home after five years
narration: Friends warned Rizal not to go home: the Noli had made him powerful enemies. He went anyway. He wanted to treat his mother's eyes, to see his family, and to learn for himself what the novel had done to his people. He sailed from Marseille on 3 July 1887, changed ships at Saigon, and reached Manila on the night of 5 August. On 8 August he was back in Calamba.

He turned part of the ground floor of the family house into a clinic. His first patient was his mother. Sources disagree about what he did: Craig wrote that he removed her cataracts, but other accounts say they were not yet ready for surgery and he only treated her. Either way, word spread that a doctor trained in Europe had come home, and patients came from all over Luzon. People called him "Doctor Uliman", from alemán, Spanish for German, because they thought he was a German doctor. He charged little, but in seven months he earned about five thousand pesos.

chapters.title: A bodyguard from the Governor
narration: Soon the Governor-General, Emilio Terrero, summoned Rizal to Malacañang Palace. Copies of the Noli had reached Manila, and Terrero wanted to read it for himself. He was a fair-minded man, and he feared Rizal would be attacked by people the novel had offended. So he gave him a bodyguard: a young Spanish lieutenant, José Taviel de Andrade.

The guard and the guarded became friends. They shared a love of painting and fencing, and together they climbed Mount Makiling and planted a flag at the top, as European climbers did. Rizal's enemies spread the story that he had raised a German flag and claimed the islands for Germany. The rumour shows how wild the talk about him had become.
The censors had advised the Governor-General to deal harshly with the author. Terrero read the book himself and set that advice aside, at least for a time.

chapters.title: A banned book
narration: The novel's enemies moved fast. The Archbishop of Manila sent a copy to the rector of the University of Santo Tomas, whose faculty judged it heretical, impious and scandalous. A government censorship board, led by a friar, recommended that it be banned. Pamphlets were printed to attack it, and in Spain it was denounced in the Senate. Owning the Noli became dangerous.

But it also had defenders. Liberals in Spain spoke up for it. In Manila, a Filipino priest, Father Vicente García, answered its critics under a pen name. In homes across the country, people read it in secret, buried it in their gardens, and dug it up to read aloud. Even a cousin of Rizal's came to complain that she had been mocked in the book. He told her the novel was a mirror: anyone who saw themselves in it should correct their faults.

chapters.title: The land and the hacienda
narration: Calamba's land belonged to a large Dominican estate, the hacienda, and the town's farmers, the Mercados among them, were its tenants. When the government asked for information about the friar estates and the taxes they paid, Rizal helped the farmers gather careful, honest facts and wrote the town's report. It listed their grievances calmly: rents raised without reason, the estate growing to swallow land that had been the town's, and tenants punished for small delays.

The report angered the friars, and the danger to Rizal's family grew. He had begun a second novel, El Filibusterismo, in Calamba that October. Terrero advised him to leave the country for his own safety and theirs. On 3 February 1888 he sailed again, this time for Hong Kong.

He also opened a gymnasium in Calamba for the young men of the town, hoping to draw them away from cockfighting and gambling toward sports and fencing. To the friars and their allies, every new activity he started looked like a plot.

He admired how clean and honest the country was, but disliked seeing men pull other people in rickshaws. He became close to Usui Seiko, called O-Sei-san, who showed him the city and helped him with the language. He thought for a while of staying, but his work for his country came first. On 13 April 1888 he sailed from Yokohama on the steamer Belgic, bound for America.

chapters.title: A guest of the Legation
narration: Rizal stopped first in Hong Kong, where he met José María Basa, a Filipino exiled after 1872, and visited nearby Macao. On 28 February 1888 he reached Yokohama, and soon went on to Tokyo. A few moments after he reached his hotel, an official of the Spanish Legation called on him and invited him to live at the Legation. Rizal accepted. It was cheaper than a hotel, and, as he wrote to a friend, if the Spaniards wanted to keep an eye on him, he had nothing to hide.
He stayed in Japan about six weeks and travelled to nearby provinces, sometimes alone, sometimes with the Spanish official or an interpreter.
In Hong Kong he was impressed by how the British colony's schools taught their pupils, and he visited the Chinese theatre, comparing its plays with the religious plays of the Philippines.

chapters.title: Learning Japan
narration: He learned to speak Japanese well enough that, with his looks, people found it hard to believe he was not Japanese. He studied the Japanese theatre, kabuki, and Japanese art, and sketched in the Japanese style. He noticed much to admire: clean streets, polite and hard-working people, and how rarely there was theft. He was moved by the beauty of the gardens and the cherry blossoms of spring.

Some things troubled him. He disliked seeing men pull other men in rickshaws, like animals. He was also struck by how quickly Japan was modernising while keeping its own culture, a lesson he hoped his own country could learn. He received several offers of work, including one at the Legation, and turned them all down.

Japan was then in the middle of the Meiji era of reforms. Only twenty years earlier it had been closed to most foreigners; now it was building railways, schools, factories and a modern army at astonishing speed, while keeping its own language, religion and customs. To a Filipino it was proof that an Asian nation could modernise on its own terms.

chapters.title: O-Sei-san
narration: In Tokyo he met Usui Seiko, a young Japanese woman whom he called O-Sei-san. She spoke English and French as well as Japanese, and she became his guide, interpreter and teacher. Together they visited museums, libraries, gardens and shrines, and she helped him with the language and the customs.

They grew very close. Rizal wrote of her with deep affection in his diary. For a while he thought of staying in Japan, where he had friends, work and a quiet life. But he believed his duty was to his own country, and that a comfortable life far away would mean abandoning it.
Their friendship is known mostly from Rizal's own diary. Usui Seiko later married an Englishman, Alfred Charlton, a teacher, and lived in Japan.

chapters.title: Sayonara
narration: On 13 April 1888 Rizal sailed from Yokohama on the steamer Belgic, bound for San Francisco. On board he met a family whose mother was half Filipino, a daughter of an Englishman named Jackson. Her son asked whether he knew "Richal", the author of Noli Me Tangere. Rizal smiled, said he did, and had to admit he was the author when the family began to praise the book.

He also met Tetcho Suehiro, a Japanese journalist and novelist who had been jailed for his writing and was going into exile in Europe. Suehiro spoke only Japanese, so Rizal acted as his interpreter all the way to London. Two writers who had both been in trouble with their governments crossed America together.
Of all his travels, Craig writes, Rizal counted his month in Japan among the happiest. He sailed away with a full diary, a little Japanese, and a heavy heart.

chapters.title: Held in the bay
narration: The Belgic reached San Francisco on 28 April 1888, but no one was allowed to land. The ship was held in quarantine, in isolation out in the bay, for about a week. The officials spoke of a disease from Asia, though no one on board was sick. Rizal suspected the real reason was politics. More than six hundred Chinese workers were on board, and the United States had recently passed a law to keep Chinese labourers out of the country.

He noticed something else: the ship's valuable cargo of silk was taken ashore at once, without any delay. Goods could land; people could not. On 4 May the first-class passengers, Rizal among them, were finally allowed ashore. He stayed at the Palace Hotel, one of the grandest in the city.
Rizal described the quarantine in his letters, and the historian James Sobredo quotes one of them in his account of the episode.

chapters.title: Across a continent
narration: On 6 May he took the ferry to Oakland and boarded a train across the continent. He passed through Sacramento and Reno, across Utah and over the Rocky Mountains, whose scenery he found magnificent, then on through Nebraska to Chicago. In Chicago he noticed that almost every cigar store had a wooden statue of a Native American outside, no two alike. It made him think how America kept the memory of its first people in public view, while at home Filipinos could learn about their own ancestors only in foreign museums.

At Niagara Falls he felt the awe that everyone feels there, though he loyally said the waterfalls of his own province were more delicate. From Albany the train ran beside the Hudson River, which reminded him of the Pasig. On 13 May he reached New York. He visited relics of George Washington, whom he called a great man without equal in that century.
The railway line across the continent had been finished only in 1869. A journey that once took months by wagon now took about a week.

chapters.title: Two Americas
narration: Rizal admired much of what he saw: the country's size and wealth, its splendid buildings and modern industry, and its energetic people. He wrote that the Americans had magnificent ideals, and that America was a homeland for the poor who were willing to work.

But he also saw the other side. The country that spoke so proudly of freedom did not give it equally to everyone. Chinese immigrants were kept out by law, and Black Americans and other people of colour faced laws and customs that treated them as inferior. He concluded that America offered freedom, but not true equality, and above all for white people. A Filipino under Spanish rule knew what it meant to be judged by race.

Ten years later this same country would rule the Philippines. His impressions show how he judged nations: not by their wealth or power, but by how they treated ordinary people, and whether their laws applied to everyone.

chapters.title: To Liverpool
narration: On 16 May 1888 he sailed from New York on the City of Rome, one of the largest steamers in the world. On board, the passengers even printed their own newspaper. He spent his spare hours rereading Gulliver's Travels in English, and kept interpreting for his Japanese friend. Other passengers were astonished that he could speak to each of them in their own language.

He landed in Liverpool on 24 May and went on to London. Ten years later, in 1898, the United States would take the Philippines from Spain, just as Jagor had predicted. In an essay written in 1889, Rizal had already wondered whether America might one day look across the Pacific.

stops.title: The British Museum
stops.teaser: Annotating an old history of the islands

He added his own notes to show that Filipinos had a culture, trade and writing before the Spanish arrived. In March 1889 he moved to Paris, where the book would be published.

chapters.title: Two rooms on Chalcot Crescent
narration: Rizal reached London in late May 1888. For a short time he stayed with Antonio María Regidor, a Filipino lawyer who had been exiled after 1872 and now practised in London. Then he rented two rooms from the Beckett family at 37 Chalcot Crescent, in Primrose Hill. Mr. Beckett was the organist of a nearby church; with his wife and three daughters, the family soon treated their lodger as a favourite. Regent's Park and the zoo were close by, and the British Museum was within walking distance.

He stayed nearly ten months, the longest he lived anywhere in Europe outside Spain. He perfected his English, read The Times, and watched how the British ran their courts and their press. A blue plaque on the house remembers him today, placed there in 1983 to mark the home of a famous visitor to the city.
His first letters home spoke of breathing the free air of England, where newspapers criticised the government openly and courts protected even the poor.

chapters.title: The Reading Room
narration: He had come to London for one reason: the British Museum. Its great circular Reading Room, under a high dome, held books on the Philippines that could not be found in Manila or even in Spain. A reader needed a good reason and a recommendation to be admitted; his came from Dr. Reinhold Rost, the librarian of the India Office and a scholar of many languages, who became a friend.

There he found a rare copy of a history of the Philippines published in Mexico in 1609: Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas, by Antonio de Morga. Morga had been a high official and judge in Manila, and he wrote from what he had seen himself, only a few decades after the Spanish arrived. Because the book was so rare, Rizal copied it out by hand, page after page, day after day.

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: Morga saw the islands with his own eyes, so soon after the Spaniards came. This is the witness I need.

fact.text: Morga's history was printed in Mexico in 1609, less than fifty years after Legazpi reached Cebu.

chapters.title: A history to be proud of
narration: Rizal's plan was to republish Morga with his own notes. Many Spanish writers described Filipinos as a backward people whom Spain had raised up. Morga's account, read carefully, showed something else. Before the Spaniards came, Filipinos had their own writing system, traded with China, Japan and their neighbours, worked metal, built ships, and had laws and leaders of their own.

In his notes Rizal set out to prove this, comparing Morga with other early accounts, many by non-Spanish writers. He argued that the islands had declined under colonial rule, not risen from nothing. Some days the prejudice he read made him angry. In the evenings at Regidor's home, the older man urged patience, and Rizal would repeat a favourite proverb: "To understand all is to forgive all."

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: They say Spain brought us civilisation. Morga shows we already had our own.

chapters.title: Letters from London
narration: From London he kept up a steady stream of writing. In February 1889 he wrote, in Tagalog, a long letter to a group of young women of Malolos, Bulacan, who had bravely asked the Governor-General for permission to open a night school where they could learn Spanish. He praised their courage and urged Filipino women to educate themselves, to think for themselves, and to raise children who would do the same. That same month Filipino reformers in Barcelona founded a newspaper, La Solidaridad, and Rizal began writing for it.

He also published a set of Tagalog proverbs and riddles in English, in a London journal. One of them reads: "Low words are stronger than loud words." But his happy life with the Becketts grew complicated: he felt that one of the daughters was becoming too fond of him, and he did not feel free to marry. In March 1889 he left for Paris, giving the family a clay medallion he had made with the profiles of the three sisters.

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: To the women of Malolos: you have shown that Filipinas, too, can stand up for learning.

fact.text: The English versions of the proverbs are Rizal's own, published in 1889.

stops.title: Paris, 1889
stops.story: Rizal moved to Paris in March 1889, the year of the Exposition Universelle, a world's fair held from May to October. Its star was the brand-new Eiffel Tower. Rizal gathered his Filipino friends in Paris into a club. They first called it the Kidlat Club, because it would last only as long as the fair, like lightning. Then, after seeing Native Americans riding proudly in Buffalo Bill's show, they renamed themselves the Indios Bravos, the Brave Indios. Spaniards used 'indio' as an insult; Rizal wanted his friends to wear it with pride and to excel in study and sport. He also finished his annotated edition of Morga's history. chapters.title: The year of the Exposition
narration: Rizal moved to Paris in March 1889, just as the city prepared for the Exposition Universelle, a world's fair held from May to October to mark one hundred years since the French Revolution. Its centrepiece was brand new: the Eiffel Tower, then the tallest structure on Earth. Millions came to see machines, art and peoples from every corner of the world.

He chose Paris partly because the Morga could be printed well there. He stayed at first with his friend Valentín Ventura, a wealthy Filipino trained in law, and then in a small room of his own. He also had a larger plan: to gather scholars of the Philippines from many countries into an international association, with Blumentritt as its president, and to hold a congress during the fair. The congress never took place.

chapters.title: Kidlat and the Indios Bravos

On 19 March 1889 they called it the Kidlat Club, kidlat meaning lightning, because it was meant to last only as long as the fair: a flash, and gone. Then, at the fair, they watched Buffalo Bill's Wild West show, where Native Americans rode and performed with great pride and skill. It gave Rizal an idea.

Spaniards often used the word indio, Indian, as an insult for Filipinos. Rizal proposed that they take the insult and wear it with pride, as the riders in the show did. The club became the Indios Bravos, the Brave Indians. Its members promised to excel in study and in sports, to prove that Filipinos were the equal of anyone. Biographers add that Rizal also formed a smaller, secret circle with a larger aim: the redemption of the Malay peoples.
The show was run by William Cody, the famous Buffalo Bill, and was one of the great attractions of the fair.

chapters.title: Morga, annotated
narration: In 1890 his edition of Morga's Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas was printed in Paris by Garnier Hermanos, with a prologue by Blumentritt. Rizal dedicated it to the Filipinos. He wrote that if the book could awaken in them an awareness of their past, he would consider his work worthwhile, and that they could then judge the present and the future.

Blumentritt praised the work but also gave honest criticism. He warned that Rizal sometimes judged the past by the ideas of the present, and was too quick to blame every problem on Spain and the friars. It was a fair point, and one that historians still argue about. The printing itself had problems: when Rizal went back to London to check the proofs, the original book was in use, and some errors slipped through.
He backed his notes with references to other early writers, many of them not Spanish, so that readers could check his claims for themselves.

chapters.title: A century hence
narration: In La Solidaridad he published some of his most famous essays. In "Filipinas dentro de cien años" (The Philippines a Century Hence), which appeared from late 1889 into 1890, he looked ahead and argued that Spain could not hold the islands forever unless it granted real reforms. He even wondered whether a power across the Pacific, the United States, might one day take an interest in them. In another piece, "Por teléfono", he mocked a friar who had led the attack on his novel.

On Sundays he fenced at Juan Luna's house; one of his opponents was Nellie Boustead, a skilled fencer whose family he would soon visit. But Paris was expensive and full of distractions, and he had a second novel to write. On 28 January 1890 he left for Brussels.
La Solidaridad came out twice a month. It was read by liberals in Spain and, smuggled in, by Filipinos at home, and Rizal's essays in it were among its most widely discussed.

chapters.title: A quieter city
narration: Early in 1890 Rizal moved to Brussels, the capital of Belgium, to live cheaply and write. He lodged in a boarding house run by two sisters, Suzanne and Marie Jacoby, at 38 Rue Philippe de Champagne. The younger sister grew fond of her lodger, and wrote to him affectionately after he left.
He kept a strict routine: writing, reading in the library, and exercise at a gymnasium and a shooting club. He was a fine shot and a fair swordsman, skills that would matter later that year.
From Brussels he wrote home often, and his letters show how anxious he was about Calamba, where the quarrel with the estate was coming to a head.

chapters.title: On the indolence of the Filipinos
narration: In Brussels he worked on his second novel, El Filibusterismo, and wrote for La Solidaridad. His longest essay, "Sobre la indolencia de los filipinos" (On the Indolence of the Filipinos), appeared in five parts from July to September 1890. Spanish writers often claimed that Filipinos were lazy by nature. Rizal did not deny that there was indolence, but he asked why.

His answers were historical. The hot climate demanded rest. Wars, pirate raids and forced labour had drained the population. Trade with neighbouring countries had been cut off, and farming discouraged. Gambling was encouraged, education was poor, and a man who worked hard often saw the fruits of his labour taken from him. Indolence, he concluded, was not in Filipino blood; it was the result of how they had been treated, and it could be cured.

He drew on Morga and other early writers to make his case: before Spanish rule, they described Filipinos busy with farming, weaving, mining, shipbuilding and trade. If Filipinos had been hard-working then, something must have changed since.

chapters.title: Bad news from Calamba
narration: From home came terrible news. The Mercado family's quarrel with the Dominican estate had begun, Rizal later said, with a turkey. The estate's manager often asked his father for a turkey for important guests. One season, disease killed most of the birds, and his father had none to spare. The angry manager raised the family's rent, then doubled it. When his father refused to pay, the estate took him to court.

The family lost the case. Other tenants who had followed their example lost too. In 1890 and 1891 the Governor-General, Valeriano Weyler, sent soldiers to Calamba. Families were evicted, their houses torn down, and those who stayed were forbidden to shelter them. Paciano and several of Rizal's brothers-in-law were deported to the island of Mindoro. Rizal wanted to rush home, but friends warned that he would only be arrested.
Weyler would later become notorious in Cuba, where his harsh methods earned him the nickname "the Butcher". Rizal's parents found shelter on a piece of land the family owned at Los Baños.

chapters.title: Rivals in Madrid
narration: In August 1890 he went to Madrid to seek justice for his family from the Spanish government. He got nowhere. Madrid brought other troubles too. When the writer Wenceslao Retana claimed in print that the Rizal family had not paid their rent, Rizal challenged him to a duel. Retana published an apology instead. He nearly fought a duel with his friend Antonio Luna, too, over a remark about a lady; Luna withdrew it.

Among the Filipinos in Madrid, a rivalry had grown between those who followed Rizal and those who followed Marcelo H. del Pilar, editor of La Solidaridad. In January 1891 the Filipino community voted on who should lead them. Rizal won, but he refused the post rather than divide his countrymen, and left Madrid. He headed south to Biarritz to rest.
Soon afterwards he stopped writing for La Solidaridad, leaving the paper to del Pilar. The two men had worked for the same cause, but they disagreed on how the campaign should be run from Madrid.

chapters.title: A rest by the sea
narration: In February 1891, tired and discouraged, Rizal went to Biarritz, a resort town on the Atlantic coast of France, close to the Spanish border. He stayed as a guest of the Boustead family at their winter home, the Villa Eliada. Mr. Eduardo Boustead had been born in the Philippines; his family were merchants with ties to Singapore and Manila, and he had long admired Rizal.

Rizal arrived carrying a private sorrow. For years he had loved Leonor Rivera, a cousin in the Philippines, and they had written to each other faithfully. But her letters had stopped, and he learned that she was to marry an Englishman. Many accounts say her mother, who feared Rizal's reputation, had kept his letters from her.

Biarritz had become a fashionable resort since the French Empress Eugénie built a palace there in the 1850s. In winter it was quiet, which suited a tired writer. His romance with Leonor had lasted about eleven years, most of them by letter.

chapters.title: Nellie

It did not work out. Nellie, a Protestant, wanted him to give up his Catholic faith and join her church, which he would not do. Her mother, too, did not favour a match with a man who had no fortune and many enemies. They parted as friends. In a farewell letter she wished him well and hoped he would find someone more worthy of him.

chapters.title: "I have finished my book!"
narration: Rizal turned back to his writing. In the quiet villa, with the Atlantic outside the window, he worked on the second novel he had begun in Calamba in 1887 and carried through London, Paris and Brussels. On 29 March 1891, the day before he left Biarritz, he finished the manuscript of El Filibusterismo.

He wrote to Blumentritt that day to share the news. Some historians, among them Ambeth Ocampo, point out that he went on to finish the clean copy for the printer in Brussels in April, so the book was finished in two senses, in two cities. On 30 March he left for Paris, then returned to Brussels.
The novel had taken him three and a half years of travel and interruptions, from Calamba in October 1887 to the Atlantic coast.

chapters.title: A darker story
narration: El Filibusterismo continues the story of the Noli thirteen years later. Its hero, Simoun, is a rich and mysterious jeweller who has the ear of the Governor-General. He is really Crisóstomo Ibarra, the hero of the first novel, returned in disguise. Having failed to win reform by peaceful means, he now uses his wealth to encourage corruption and plot a bloody revolution, hoping that a rotten government will collapse.

His plot fails. At the end, dying, he confesses to a Filipino priest, Padre Florentino, who tells him that freedom cannot be won by hatred and crime, only by virtue, sacrifice and love. The priest throws Simoun's jewels into the sea. The book is darker and angrier than the Noli, and its warning runs both ways: to Spain, that injustice breeds revolution, and to Filipinos, that a revolution without virtue only trades one tyranny for another.

Even the title was a provocation. In the Philippines a filibustero meant an enemy of Spain, a subversive. Rizal explained to Blumentritt that it was a dangerous word: a filibustero was a patriot who would soon be hanged, or a fool who presumed to think for himself.

chapters.title: Cheaper printers
narration: On 5 July 1891 Rizal moved to Ghent, an old Belgian university city with canals, guild houses and printers who charged less than those in Brussels. He shared lodgings with a young Filipino engineering student, José Alejandrino, and to save money the two bought their own food and cooked their own meals.
He found a printer, F. Meyer-Van Loo, on Vlaanderenstraat, who agreed to print El Filibusterismo and to be paid in parts as the work went on. Rizal handed over the manuscript and every peso he had.

Rizal arrived in a gloomy mood. The news from Calamba was bad, his hopes of Madrid were gone, and he had lost both Leonor and Nellie. Work was his refuge. Alejandrino would later become a general in the revolution and write a memoir about these years.

By early August the printer had to stop: the novel lay half printed. In despair, Rizal thought of throwing the manuscript into the fire, as he once had in Berlin.
Then help came, again, from a friend. Valentín Ventura in Paris heard of his trouble and sent money, and the presses started again.
