chapters.title: 18 September 1891
narration: On 18 September 1891 El Filibusterismo came off the press. Rizal sent the first copies to friends in Hong Kong, among them José María Basa, and to reformers in Europe. To Valentín Ventura he gave the original manuscript and an autographed printed copy, in thanks.

He dedicated the book to the memory of the three priests executed in 1872, Mariano Gómez, José Burgos and Jacinto Zamora. The Church, he wrote, by refusing to strip them of their priesthood, had cast doubt on the crime they were accused of; the government, by surrounding their trial with mystery, had made people believe there had been an error. He dedicated his work to them as victims of the evil he was fighting. The dedication gives the date of their execution as 28 February 1872; in fact it was 17 February, a slip that historians have long noted.
He sent copies to Hong Kong on purpose: many Filipino exiles lived there, and from there the book could be smuggled into Manila on the regular steamers.

chapters.title: Why so dark?
narration: The Fili was written in the worst years of Rizal's life so far. While he wrote it, his family was driven from their land, his brother and brothers-in-law were deported, and his hopes for reform from Madrid were dashed. The darkness of the book reflects that time.

Yet it is not a call to blind revolt. It shows where injustice leads, and warns what a revolution without virtue would become. Rizal now believed his place was closer to home. He left Europe for good, sailing from Marseille on 18 October 1891 aboard the Melbourne, bound for Hong Kong, where he could be near his family and his people.

Like the Noli, the Fili was written in Spanish and was banned in the Philippines; copies were smuggled in and passed from hand to hand. For years afterwards Filipinos who wanted change argued over its meaning. Was Simoun a warning, or a model?

In Hong Kong he planned to practise as an eye doctor and to bring his family to live with him, away from their persecutors. He also nursed an older dream: a modern Filipino school, and Craig records that a young Pampangan had once offered him a large sum to found one in Hong Kong.

stops.story: Rizal left Europe and reached Hong Kong, then a British colony, on 20 November 1891. He operated on his mother's eye, and she could read again. He also made a plan to move Filipino families to North Borneo and start a farming colony there, but it came to nothing. In June 1892 he decided to go home to Manila, knowing it was dangerous. Today plaques mark both his clinic and his house.

chapters.title: A new start
narration: Rizal reached Hong Kong, then a British colony on the coast of China, on 20 November 1891. The Filipino community there, many of them exiles of 1872 like José María Basa, welcomed him. He was licensed to practise medicine in the colony and opened an eye clinic at No. 5 D'Aguilar Street, in the busy Central district.

Patients came quickly: Chinese, British, Portuguese and Filipino. A Portuguese doctor, Lorenzo P. Márquez, became a close friend and sent him patients. For the first time in years, Rizal earned a good living from his profession. Today a plaque put up by the Hong Kong government marks the site of his clinic.

He also read old newspapers in the colony's library and wrote articles on the Philippines for the Hong Kong Telegraph, whose editor became a friend. Copies of the paper were mailed to Manila, until the Spanish censors caught on and banned it.

chapters.title: Christmas together
narration: Then his family came. Driven out of Calamba, his father, Paciano and several of his sisters joined him in Hong Kong. His mother came too, after yet another ordeal: she had been arrested in Manila on a petty charge, for no longer using one of her surnames, and ordered to walk to Calamba for trial. Her guards, ashamed, carried her in a hammock instead. The charge was dropped.

The family lived together at No. 2 Rednaxela Terrace, a street whose name is "Alexander" spelled backwards. Christmas 1891 was one of the happiest of Rizal's life: after years apart, almost all of them were together again. And he could finally do what he had trained for. He operated on his mother's eye, and she was able to see and read again.

chapters.title: A new Calamba in Borneo
narration: Rizal had a plan for the families evicted from Calamba: to move them to British North Borneo, now Sabah, and start a farming colony where they could work their own land in peace. In March 1892 he sailed to Sandakan and looked over land the British North Borneo Company offered. The company wanted farmers who could grow abacá, coconuts and sugarcane, crops the Calamba families knew well.

But the Governor-General of the Philippines, Eulogio Despujol, disapproved. He argued that the Philippines needed its own farmers at home. The plan came to nothing. Meanwhile Rizal kept writing: an appeal to the Spanish nation on behalf of Calamba, a Tagalog version of the Rights of Man, and a draft constitution for a new society he wanted to found at home: La Liga Filipina.

After visiting the colony's prison with Dr. Márquez, he wrote an article contrasting British punishment, meant to reform prisoners, with Spanish punishment, which he saw as meant only to make them suffer.

lines.speaker: rizal
lines.text: A new Calamba, under a fairer flag. If Spain will not give them land, Borneo will.

chapters.title: The decision
narration: In June 1892 the Spanish consul in Hong Kong assured Rizal that he could safely return to Manila. His friends begged him not to go. He went anyway. He wanted to discuss the Borneo plan with Despujol, to found his society, and above all to stop the persecution of his family and friends, which he believed would continue as long as he stayed away.

Before leaving he wrote two letters and left them with Dr. Márquez, marked "To be opened after my death". One was to his family, the other to the Filipino people. In them he wrote that he was going not to atone for any crime, but to complete his work and to set the example he had always preached. On 21 June 1892 he sailed with his sister Lucía. Craig records that on the very day his travel papers were issued, a secret case was opened against him in Manila.
His friends in Hong Kong, Basa among them, begged him not to go.

chapters.title: Back in Manila
narration: Rizal landed in Manila at noon on Sunday, 26 June 1892. Officers met him at the pier, and his luggage was searched at the custom house. He took Room 22 of the Hotel Oriente, which looked out on the church of Binondo. That afternoon he called on the Governor-General, Eulogio Despujol, who told him to come back at seven in the evening.

In a series of meetings over the next days, Despujol agreed to pardon Rizal's father, and later to let his exiled relatives return. Rizal wrote down every meeting in detail, with dates and times, in an account he later sent secretly to friends.

Despujol had arrived promising reforms, and at first seemed to keep his word. Rizal believed he meant well. Years later, Craig read the government's confidential files and concluded that the Governor-General had been preparing to deport Rizal from the start.

chapters.title: A journey north
narration: On Monday at six in the morning he took the new railway north. He visited Malolos, San Fernando and Tarlac, stopping at Bacolor on the way back, and returned to Manila on Tuesday afternoon. He met friends and supporters along the way.

He was followed everywhere. Craig, who later read the secret police files, says that houses Rizal visited were searched soon after he left, and their owners questioned. Warned of this, Rizal's hosts hurried to hide forbidden papers. In one house, Craig writes, so many banned writings were kept that Rizal waited until the family had carried them up into the roof.

At one house, Craig tells us, the host did not know who his guest was. He began to talk about Rizal, declaring that the author of the Noli had a charmed life and could appear among them at that very moment if he wished. When Rizal told him who he was, the old man hurried off to hide his papers before the search he knew would follow.

chapters.title: La Liga Filipina
narration: On the evening of 3 July 1892, Rizal met with a group of Filipino patriots at the house of Doroteo Ongjunco on Ilaya Street, in Tondo. There they founded La Liga Filipina, the Philippine League. Among those present was a young warehouse agent named Andrés Bonifacio.

Rizal had written its constitution. Its aims were: to unite the whole archipelago into one strong body; to help members in need; to defend them against violence and injustice; to encourage education, farming and trade; and to study and apply reforms. Its motto was Latin: Unus instar omnium, "One like all". It was a peaceful society. It asked for no weapons, only unity, mutual help and education.
The members elected their own officers; Rizal, its author, was not among them.

chapters.title: Arrested
narration: On Wednesday, 6 July, Rizal went again to Malacañang. This time Despujol showed him a few small printed sheets: handbills called "Pobres Frailes" (Poor Friars), which mocked the wealth of the religious orders. He said they had been found in a roll of pillows and mats packed with Rizal's luggage. Rizal said the bedding was his sister's and that he had brought no such papers. It made no difference. Despujol's nephew took him by palace carriage to Fort Santiago.

On 7 July the government announced that Rizal would be deported. That same night, Bonifacio and others, convinced that peaceful reform was now hopeless, founded a secret society for independence: the Katipunan. On 15 July Rizal sailed south on the steamer Cebu, under guard. On Sunday evening, 17 July 1892, he reached Dapitan, on the northern coast of Mindanao.

Leaflets like these circulated freely in Hong Kong. Craig concluded that they had been gathered up by accident with waste paper and packed in the bedding, and that the Governor-General used them as an excuse.

stops.title: Teacher in exile
stops.teaser: Sent far from Manila, he builds for the town
stops.story: In July 1892, days after founding La Liga Filipina in Manila, Rizal was arrested and sent into exile in Dapitan, a small town in Mindanao. He arrived on 17 July 1892. Soon after, he won a share of the government lottery and used it to buy land in Talisay, about a kilometre from the town. There he built houses of bamboo, wood and nipa. He opened a school for boys, who did chores and farm work instead of paying fees. He treated patients, and poor patients paid nothing. He built a water system for the town, drained marshes and lit the plaza. He also farmed, wrote poems and collected plants and animals for European scientists. He stayed four years.

chapters.title: Exile
narration: Rizal arrived in Dapitan, a small town on the northern coast of Mindanao, on a dark and rainy Sunday evening, 17 July 1892. The commandant, Captain Ricardo Carnicero, took charge of him. The Jesuits who ran the parish had been told they could take Rizal in if he publicly gave up his criticisms of the Church and of Spain. He refused, so he lived in the commandant's house instead.

Carnicero was supposed to watch him closely. Instead, the two men became friends. Rizal was free to walk around the town, and he wrote a poem in Carnicero's honour. His first letters from Dapitan describe the place almost happily: a good climate, a quiet life, and only his family and his books missing.
He would spend four years there, longer than he lived in any other place as an adult.

lines.text: A quiet town, a good climate. If only my family and my books were here.

chapters.title: The lottery and Talisay
narration: In September 1892 the mail steamer arrived flying flags, and Carnicero rushed to the beach with a band, thinking an important official had come. Instead, the steamer brought news: a lottery ticket that Rizal had bought together with Carnicero and a Spaniard living nearby had won the second prize, twenty thousand pesos. Rizal's share was about six thousand.

He sent part to his father and part to his friend Basa in Hong Kong, and used the rest to buy land at Talisay, a little bay about a kilometre from the town. There he built a small settlement of houses made of bamboo, wood and nipa: one for himself, one for his pupils, a clinic and others. He planted abacá, coconuts, fruit trees, cacao and coffee, brought in modern farm tools, and went into business with local traders in fishing and abacá.

chapters.title: The school in the hammock
narration: Rizal opened a school for the boys of Dapitan. It began with three pupils and grew to more than a dozen. There were no fees. Instead, the boys worked in his garden, on the farm and on building projects. In the afternoons he taught from a hammock: reading, writing, Spanish and English, arithmetic and geometry, geography, history and nature study. Each day was set aside for one language, and anyone who spoke another was teased with a mock handcuff of rattan.

The boys also learned by doing. They helped collect plants, shells, insects and reptiles for European museums, and practised swimming, shooting and fencing. Rizal paid them for their work with clothes, books and other useful gifts. Craig called it the first school of its kind in the islands, mixing English, nature study and practical training.

chapters.title: Doctor, engineer, scientist
narration: Patients came to Talisay from all over Mindanao and beyond. The poor paid nothing; the rich paid well. When a wealthy Englishman paid him five hundred pesos, Rizal used the money to light the streets of the town. With his former Ateneo teacher, Father Francisco Sánchez, who visited Dapitan, he surveyed the land and planned a water system: a dam to collect water from a stream, and pipes to carry it to the houses. In the town plaza they built a large raised map of Mindanao to teach geography.

He collected animals and plants for European scientists, and three were named after him: a flying lizard, Draco rizali; a beetle, Apogonia rizali; and a frog, Rhacophorus rizali. In 1895 an Irish woman, Josephine Bracken, came to Dapitan, and she and Rizal lived together. In mid-1896 Dr. Pío Valenzuela came on behalf of the Katipunan to tell him a revolution was being prepared. Rizal said it was premature: the people were not ready and had no arms. On 31 July 1896, after four years in Dapitan, he left to volunteer as a doctor in Cuba.

stops.title: Fort Santiago
stops.story: In 1896 Rizal was allowed to leave Dapitan to serve as a volunteer doctor in Cuba. While he was at sea, revolution broke out in the Philippines. He was arrested on board, held in Barcelona, and shipped back to Manila, arriving on 3 November 1896. He was locked in Fort Santiago. On 26 December a military court tried him for rebellion, sedition and illegal association. He could not question the witnesses, and he was sentenced to death. On 29 December he was moved to the prison chapel. That day he finished a poem of fourteen stanzas, a farewell to his country. He hid it inside a small alcohol stove and gave the stove to his sister Trinidad, saying in English, "There is something inside." The poem is now known as Mi Último Adiós.

chapters.title: A doctor for Cuba
narration: Blumentritt had written to Rizal about the war in Cuba, where many Spanish soldiers were dying of disease and there were too few doctors. Rizal offered to serve there as a volunteer army doctor, and the Governor-General, Ramón Blanco, accepted. On 31 July 1896 he left Dapitan. Reaching Manila on 6 August, he had just missed the mail steamer to Spain, so he waited for the next one aboard a Spanish cruiser, the Castilla, in Manila Bay, where he was treated as a guest.

While he waited, in late August, the Katipunan launched the revolution. Fighting broke out around Manila. Blanco gave Rizal letters of recommendation stating that he had nothing to do with the uprising. On 3 September 1896 Rizal sailed for Spain on the Isla de Panay.

chapters.title: Arrested at sea
narration: On 30 September, at sea, the captain told him he was to be arrested on arrival. On 3 October the ship reached Barcelona, and Rizal was held in the castle of Montjuïc. There he was interviewed by the commander of the region: Despujol, the same man who had exiled him in 1892. He was then shipped back to Manila on the Colón.

Friends in London tried to save him. When the ship stopped at Singapore, a British colony, they asked the court there to free him, arguing he was being held without any charge. The judge refused, ruling that the ship was Spanish territory. Rizal never knew of the attempt. On 3 November 1896 he reached Manila and was locked in Fort Santiago.
He was held at Montjuïc only a few hours, until the mail steamer for Manila was ready to sail.

chapters.title: The trial
narration: The authorities tried to build a case against him. His brother Paciano was cruelly treated to make him sign a statement that José led the rebellion; he refused. Rizal was questioned in November. He was allowed to choose a defender only from a list of army officers. He recognised one name: Luis Taviel de Andrade, brother of the lieutenant who had guarded him in 1887. Taviel defended him bravely, at some risk to himself.

On 26 December 1896 a military court met at the Cuartel de España in Intramuros. Rizal was charged with rebellion, sedition and illegal association. He could not question the witnesses whose statements were used against him. He wrote his own defence, arguing that he had advised against the revolution and had never been its leader. The court sentenced him to death. The new Governor-General, Camilo de Polavieja, confirmed the sentence on 28 December.

In his defence he pointed out that he had refused to support the rising when Valenzuela came to Dapitan, and that, sailing home as a prisoner, he could have tried to escape at Singapore but had not, because his conscience was clear.

chapters.title: The last poem
narration: On the morning of 29 December he was moved to the prison chapel. Jesuit priests who had taught him at the Ateneo visited him, and so did his mother and sisters. He was not allowed close to them. To his sister Trinidad he gave a small alcohol cooking stove, a gift he had once received in Paris, and said quickly in English, so the guard would not understand: "There is something inside."

Inside was a poem of fourteen stanzas, written in Spanish, without a title. It is known today as Mi Último Adiós, My Last Farewell. His family found it at home after he was gone. Accounts written later disagree about some events of that last night, including whether he took back his criticism of the Church and whether he married Josephine Bracken. Historians still debate these questions, and good sources take both sides seriously.
That night he also wrote farewell letters to his family.

stops.title: His final day
stops.story: Early on the morning of 30 December 1896, José Rizal was taken from Fort Santiago and walked to Bagumbayan, the open field beside Manila Bay. There, at about seven o'clock, he was executed. He was thirty-five years old. His death did not end the struggle for freedom; it made it stronger. Within two years the Philippines declared its independence. The field where he died is now Rizal Park, also called the Luneta, and his monument stands there, guarded day and night. Every 30 December the country remembers him on Rizal Day. His novels, his poems, his letters and the places he lived are still with us, and so are the questions he asked about justice, education and love of country. This is the last stop on his journey.

chapters.title: Dawn, 30 December
narration: Early on the morning of 30 December 1896, José Rizal left Fort Santiago for the last time. He walked to Bagumbayan, the open field outside the city walls beside Manila Bay, accompanied by his defender, Luis Taviel de Andrade, and two Jesuit priests. Soldiers lined the way, and crowds had gathered to watch.

He was dressed in a dark suit. Those who walked with him said he was calm, and spoke quietly about the clear morning and the view across the bay. It was the same field where, almost twenty-five years before, the three priests Gómez, Burgos and Zamora had been executed.

The night before, he had written his last letters. To Blumentritt he wrote in German, saying goodbye to his friend and declaring that he died innocent of the crime of rebellion. To Paciano he wrote that he knew how much his brother had suffered for him: "I assure you, brother, that I die innocent of this crime of rebellion."

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He walked the short road from the fort to the field, calm, on a clear December morning.

chapters.title: Seven in the morning
narration: At about 7:03 in the morning, José Rizal was executed. He was thirty-five years old.

He had been a doctor, a poet, a novelist, a scholar of history and languages, a teacher, a farmer, a sculptor and a painter. He had travelled across Asia, Europe and America, and written letters to friends in half a dozen languages. He had asked for reform, not violence. Yet he was killed as the leader of a revolution he had advised against.
By most accounts, his last words were "Consummatum est", "It is finished", the last words of Christ in the Gospel of John.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He died as he had written he would: for the country he loved.

fact.text: The Intramuros Administration gives the time as about 7:03 a.m.

chapters.title: What his death began
narration: His death did not end the struggle; it strengthened it. The revolution spread. On 12 June 1898 Filipino leaders declared the independence of the Philippines at Kawit, Cavite. Later that year the revolutionary government declared 30 December a national day of mourning for Rizal, and it has been remembered ever since as Rizal Day.

His remains were buried secretly, without a name on the grave. His family searched until they found the spot. In 1912 his remains were moved to the base of a new monument on the field where he died. Bagumbayan became the Luneta, and later Rizal Park. His monument stands there today, guarded day and night.

In a last letter he had asked for a simple grave: a stone and a cross, his name and the dates of his birth and death, nothing more. His sister Narcisa searched the cemeteries of Manila until she found the unmarked grave at Paco, and had it marked in secret. Far away in Leitmeritz, Blumentritt mourned his friend and defended his name in print for the rest of his life.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The field where he died now carries his name.

fact.text: The monument was unveiled on Rizal Day, 30 December 1913.

chapters.title: The journey goes on
narration: In 1956 the Philippine Congress passed Republic Act No. 1425, the Rizal Law. It requires every school and university in the country to teach his life, works and writings, including his two novels. The law exists because lawmakers believed that every generation of Filipinos should know the man and the questions he asked.

Those questions are still with us. What does a person owe their country? Is education the way to freedom? Can a people be free if they are not just to one another? Rizal answered them with his work: his clinic, his school, his novels and his letters. In the last stanza of his farewell, he wrote that he was going to a place without slaves or oppressors. This is the last stop on his journey. Yours goes on.

His novels have been translated into many languages. His name is on streets and schools across the country, and on a province, Rizal, east of Manila. Each year Filipinos remember him on 19 June, his birthday, and on 30 December.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For I go where no slave before the oppressor bends, where faith can never kill, and God reigns e'er on high!

fact.text: Republic Act No. 1425 was approved on 12 June 1956.
